c1.story:
Here is an odd fact about the country that runs the world's software. For three decades, most of the code written in India belonged to someone else. Engineers in Bengaluru and Pune built and maintained systems that an American bank or a German carmaker owned. Software product companies are the exception: they write a program once, own it outright, and rent it out again and again. It is the dream business model of the internet age, and the listed Indian version comes in four very different flavours.

The first door is the enterprise landlord. Oracle Financial Services Software, born as i-flex in Mumbai, sells its Flexcube core-banking system to banks across continents. Intellect Design Arena, Newgen, RateGain, Amagi and Capillary sell banking, document, hotel-pricing, broadcast and loyalty software to big companies worldwide. A deal takes a year to close. Leaving takes a decade, because ripping out a bank's core system is closer to a heart transplant than a software upgrade.

The second door is the toll booth. Every time your bank texts you a one-time password, a messaging platform like Tanla probably carried it. Every time an ad on your phone turns into an app install, Affle gets paid. Every time a shopkeeper swipes your card on a Pine Labs terminal, a tiny fee drops into the till. Nobody calls a salesman; revenue grows with the customer's volume.

The third door is the cinema: consumer internet. PhysicsWallah, which grew out of Alakh Pandey's YouTube physics lessons, and Nazara in gaming must win households one subscription or one purchase at a time, and marketing is their biggest bill.

The fourth door is the contractor with a kit of his own: Persistent's engineering services wrapped around products, MapmyIndia's maps and devices, eMudhra's digital signatures, ideaForge's drones.

Ask three questions of any software stock: who pays, how often, and how much it hurts to leave. The answers sort the doors.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four doors. Read each from the top down, then compare the bars across them.

  • The name and the line under it tell you how the money arrives: licences and subscriptions from big companies, a toll on every transaction, household purchases one at a time, or a mix of project work and product.
  • The tickers are listed names behind that door; click one to open its stock page. The enterprise tile is the most crowded, which tells you where most of India's listed product depth sits: banking and business software sold abroad.
  • The profit bar shows how much of each sale the company keeps. Enterprise sits at high because a locked-in bank pays every year with little extra cost to serve. The toll booths sit at medium: volume is great, but telcos, banks and ad networks take a cut first. Consumer internet sits at low because every new user has to be bought with marketing. The hybrid door sits at medium, earning like a services firm.
  • The last line is the bet. Note the consumer tile's: user growth turning into profit before the cash runs out. That is a race, not an annuity.

Then read the analogy under the tiles: landlord, toll booth, cinema, contractor. It is worth keeping in your head, because the so-what line is the key practical rule on this page: a toll booth and a cinema can post the same growth number and deserve very different multiples. Always identify the door before you read the growth rate.

c2.story:
Follow one piece of software from idea to invoice and you will see where the money is made and where it leaks.

It starts with an idea and a team. A product manager in Chennai notices that mid-sized banks in Africa and Southeast Asia are stuck on ageing core systems, and an engineering team writes a modern replacement that the company owns outright. This first station is where Indian listed product companies stand, and it is where all the value is created: the code, the patents, the know-how.

Then the code needs a home. Almost all modern software runs on rented servers from Amazon, Microsoft or Google. That cloud bill is the first rent paid to a foreigner, and it grows with every customer. For payments and personal data, Indian rules add a twist: since the RBI's data-localisation directive of 2018, payment data must stay on servers in India, so some of that home has to be local.

Next comes the quiet, expensive middle: building, testing, security audits and certificates. A bank will not touch a product without them, and a digital-signature or payments licence is itself a moat. Indian engineers do this well and cheaply.

Then the hardest part, getting in front of the buyer. Enterprise names need sales teams in London, Dubai and Singapore, and often a big system integrator to implement the product. Consumer apps live on Google's and Apple's stores, which take their cut. Messaging platforms need the telcos. These are the gatekeepers, and every one of them charges a toll on the toll booth.

Finally the customer, who must be earned again every year at renewal. A happy bank adds modules; an unhappy one starts a multi-year exit.

The money is made owning the code and keeping the customer. It leaks in the middle, to clouds, stores and partners.
c2.read:
The five boxes run left to right from idea to renewal. Read the top line of each box, then look at who stands there.

  • Idea and intellectual property: Indian listed product companies, with engineering in Bengaluru, Pune, Chennai and Hyderabad.
  • Cloud and infrastructure: the American clouds, plus Indian data centres where localisation demands it.
  • Build, test and compliance: Indian engineers again, and the regulators who certify them.
  • Go to market: the companies' own sales teams, but also app stores, telcos and system integrators acting as gatekeepers.
  • Customer and renewal: banks, airlines, hotels, brands, merchants and students.

Now the band row. Notice the pattern: India listed, rival, India listed, gatekeepers, customers. The Indian coloured cells appear twice, at the first and third stations, with the rival band, US clouds, sitting between them. Unlike most industries on this page, where India holds one contiguous stretch, here India's stations are interrupted by a foreign landlord.

The so-what line tells you how to read that: money is made at the first and last stations and lost in the middle. When you look at a company's accounts, the cloud bill, app-store fees and partner commissions are those middle stations showing up as cost.

The geography note adds the currency angle: engineering in Indian cities, the biggest customers in New York, London, Dubai and Singapore. Dollar revenue against rupee cost, minus two rents to foreigners, the cloud and the app store, is the whole margin story in one sentence.

c3.story:
Who actually pays an Indian software product company? Mostly not Indians. That is the first surprise in this card, and it shapes everything else.

The biggest buyers are banks and insurers around the world. A bank in Nairobi or Riyadh replacing its core system, a European insurer digitising claims, a lender automating loan documents: these are the deals that fill the order books of Oracle Financial Services, Intellect and Newgen. They move with bank technology budgets and with the slow rhythm of core-system replacement, which happens once in a generation per bank. That is a feature: one win is a decade of maintenance revenue.

Then the brands and advertisers, who buy mobile ad delivery, loyalty programmes and customer messaging. Their budgets swell around the festive season and new app launches, which is why ad-tech and messaging quarters can look lumpy. Hotels and airlines buy pricing and distribution tools and move with travel demand; RateGain's fortunes rose and fell with hotel room rates through the pandemic and after. Broadcasters and streamers buy cloud playout and ad insertion, the business Amagi built.

The domestic exceptions are where things get interesting. Merchants and fintechs buy card terminals and payment rails, and they move with card and UPI volumes. But UPI itself carries no merchant fee by government mandate since 2020, so payment firms earn on cards, devices and services around the free rail. Students and parents buy test preparation, and they move with exam calendars and household income rather than with any boardroom.

Government and defence buy digital signatures, maps and drones, in budget cycles and in bursts around border tension. Automakers and logistics firms buy navigation and fleet tracking.

This is an export industry with two domestic side doors: payments and coaching.
c3.read:
Eight tiles, eight buyer groups. Each tile has three lines: who buys, what they buy, and what moves their spending. The third line is the one to copy into your watch list.

Sort the tiles into three groups as you read:

  • Foreign corporate budgets: banks and insurers worldwide, brands and advertisers, hotels and airlines, broadcasters and streamers. Their third lines talk about technology budgets, ad spend and travel demand. This group is the bulk of the industry and moves with the global economy and the dollar.
  • Indian consumers, at one remove: merchants and fintechs, and students and parents. Their third lines mention UPI volumes, RBI fee rules, exam calendars and household income. This is the domestic engine.
  • Indian state and industry: government and defence, automakers and logistics. Budget cycles, tenders and car sales move these.

The so-what line under the grid makes the key point: this industry is less about Indian consumption and more about foreign technology budgets, with edtech and payments as the exceptions. That is the opposite of most consumer-facing Indian sectors.

Then link the tiles back to card one. The enterprise door sells mainly into the first tile and the travel and broadcast tiles. The toll-booth door sells to brands and merchants. The consumer door is students. The hybrid door covers government and automakers. A company whose tiles are all foreign is a dollar story; one whose tiles are all domestic is an India digital story, and they will not move together.

c4.story:
The explainer's analogy is the right one: a software product is a textbook written once and sold every year to a new class. Writing it costs a fortune; printing one more copy costs almost nothing. So the profit and loss of a true product company should get better as it grows, because each new customer brings revenue without bringing much extra cost. That is operating leverage, and it is what the market pays a product multiple for.

For the enterprise door, the big cost is people: engineers who build and maintain the product, salespeople who chase year-long deals, support staff who keep banks happy. If the company is a real product business, that people cost falls as a share of sales over time. If it stays stubbornly high, the company is probably billing hours for customisation, a services firm wearing a product badge.

The platform door looks completely different. A messaging company that sends a bank's OTPs pays the telco for every message. An ad platform pays publishers for the space. A payment firm pays banks and networks. All of that sits inside the headline revenue and flows straight out again. So platforms show huge revenue and thin margins, and the only honest measure is the gross margin after those pass-through costs.

For a platform, headline revenue is a vanity number. The margin after pass-through is the business.

Two accounting lines deserve suspicion. Capitalised development cost lets a company park engineer salaries on the balance sheet as an asset rather than expensing them, which flatters today's profit and returns later as amortisation. And receivables: enterprise deals are billed in milestones, banks pay slowly, and receivable days rising ahead of revenue is often the first sign that revenue is being booked faster than cash is arriving. Interest rarely matters, since most names hold net cash, but treasury income on that cash can quietly prop up the bottom line.
c4.read:
Two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of revenue down to what is left: global enterprise products on the left, platforms paid per transaction on the right. These two shapes are almost mirror images, which is the point of the card.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • People: engineers, sales and support is the input bar. In the enterprise chart it takes roughly half of every rupee: this is a business of brains. In the platform chart it takes only about a fifth.
  • Cloud hosting, marketing, partner and platform fees is the opex bar, and here the charts flip. The enterprise chart spends about a quarter. The platform chart spends well over half, because the fees it passes on to telcos, ad networks and banks sit in this bar.
  • Depreciation and interest is a sliver in both: asset-light either way.
  • What is left lands in the low twenties for enterprise and the mid teens for platforms.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes; hover a bar for the amount.

Below the charts, the list of lines tells you what to read. Four get a yes: employee cost share, gross margin after pass-through, receivables, and capitalised development. Depreciation, capex and other income get a sometimes, each with a specific trap: impairments, edtech centres and drone factories, and treasury income. Interest gets a no. The so-what line gives the one test to run on any name: employee cost falling as a share of sales, without capitalised development rising to hide it.

c5.story:
The business of selling software to banks and brands is slow and steady. The price of the shares is anything but. In this industry the cycle lives in the multiple far more than in the revenue, and the multiple takes its orders from US interest rates and from whatever the market believes about technology that month.

The boom of 2020 and 2021 had two engines. Covid pushed banks, shops, schools and advertisers online at once, so demand was real. And near-zero interest rates made investors willing to pay almost anything for growth far in the future. Freshworks, born in Chennai, listed on Nasdaq in 2021; Indian SaaS unicorns multiplied; listed product names traded at record multiples, and edtech was valued like infrastructure.

Then the Federal Reserve raised rates hard in 2022, and every distant profit got discounted more heavily. Software multiples collapsed worldwide. Indian startups entered a funding winter, Byju's went from India's most valuable startup to a cautionary tale of debt and governance, and listed names fell by half or more. The revenue of most enterprise names barely flinched. The prices did.

By 2024, cost discipline had restored margins and banking-software deal wins picked up. In 2025 the listing window flung open: PhysicsWallah, Pine Labs and a string of other product names came to market, while the online gaming ban forced write-offs and data-protection rules arrived.

And then early 2026. When Anthropic released plugins for its Claude Cowork agent, investors around the world asked whether AI agents would replace the software sold per user seat. Product stocks everywhere fell, India's included, even as their recurring revenue kept compounding. By autumn the panic had faded and the question had shifted from who is replaced by AI to who sells it.

Revenue climbed the stairs. The share price took the lift, in both directions.
c5.read:
Three pieces: the clock, the timeline and the four hands. On this card, remember that the clock describes valuations more than the businesses themselves.

The clock has four arcs clockwise from the top: boom, peak, bust and bottom. The years under them are the last full cycle: the boom of 2020 and 2021, the peak of 2021, the bust of 2022 and 2023, and the bottom of 2023 and 2024. The arrow points at the bottom arc again, labelled an AI-scare bottom. So the industry went round once, started climbing in 2024, and got knocked back to the bottom by the 2026 scare. That second dip is in the price, not the order book, which is why the label says multiples reset, deal wins continuing.

The timeline runs from 2019. Read the colours: the boom years, the bust years, then neutral entries for 2024 and 2025 despite all the noise, and the 2026 entry marked now.

The four hands:

  • US software multiples: recovering off lows, an up arrow. Indian names follow their US peers with a lag of a month or two.
  • Large deal wins at banking-software names: steady, flat. Today's deals are licence and implementation revenue for the next two years.
  • Platform volumes: ads, messages and swipes still growing, an up arrow.
  • Edtech unit economics: improving but thin, a mixed reading.

Two hands up, one flat, one mixed: the price side is healing first. The so-what line tells you who benefits: enterprise and platform doors first, because their revenue never fell, while consumer names still owe the market proof of profit.

c6.story:
Two dials set the share price, one sets the earnings, and the rest add colour.

The price setters are US technology sentiment and US interest rates. A software company's value rests on profits far in the future, so the rate used to discount those profits matters enormously. When the US ten-year yield jumped in 2022, a profit ten years out suddenly looked much smaller in today's money, and multiples collapsed everywhere from San Francisco to Pune. Sentiment works the same way faster: when American software stocks rally, Indian product names re-rate within weeks, whether or not anything changed in their own business.

The earnings setter is global bank technology budgets. For the enterprise door, the decision of a bank in Nairobi or Manila to replace its core system is the order book. Those decisions are slow and lumpy, and they matter more than any macro data point.

US rates decide what the market pays for a rupee of software profit. Bank budgets decide how many rupees there are.

Then the two-weight dials. A weaker rupee widens margins for the exporters. Indian digital ad spend lifts ad-tech and messaging volumes in step. Card and UPI spending raises payment-platform fees. And the newest dial, AI pricing anxiety, cuts against any business that charges per user seat: if an AI agent can do the work of ten users, why pay for ten seats? Usage-based platforms, which charge per ad, message or swipe, are far less exposed.

The light dials round it out. Venture funding is two-faced: it raises the market's appetite for tech, but it also funds rivals who pay engineers more and discount their products. Household incomes move coaching enrolments. And US visa and tariff policy raises onsite costs for the product-plus-services names, which still send engineers to client sites.
c6.read:
Each row is a dial: the outside force, the channel by which it reaches profits, what a rise does, its weight in dots, and today's reading where we track a series.

  • The arrow: green up means a rise helps, red down means it hurts, a diamond means it cuts both ways.
  • The dots: three means the dial can make or break a year.

Start with the three-dot rows: US technology sentiment, US interest rates and global bank technology budgets. Notice that two of the three are about valuation, not business. That is unusual, and it is the clock card's point again: in this industry the price moves more than the revenue.

Next, the reading column. Seven of the ten rows map to a series we track. Some map directly, like the US ten-year yield and the rupee. Others are stand-ins and deserve a lighter touch: the Nifty IT index stands in for US tech sentiment, the Nifty Media index for ad spend, consumer non-durables output for card and UPI spending, India VIX for venture risk appetite, and education inflation for coaching demand. Use those as direction checks, not precise gauges. Bank budgets, AI anxiety and visa policy show a dash; you read those in earnings calls and the news.

Finally, count the reds: US rates, AI anxiety, and visa and tariff policy. Two of them are about the US, one about technology itself. The only diamond is venture funding.

The so-what line distils the table: track US software multiples for the price and global bank technology budgets for the earnings.

c7.story:
Why is there no Indian Salesforce? Plenty of Indian engineers built Salesforce. The bottlenecks on this card explain why the listed Indian product sector is smaller and thinner-margined than its American cousin, and why some of its stocks blow up.

The first is the home market. Indian companies spend little on software and haggle hard over what they do buy. So any serious Indian product company has to sell abroad from almost the first day, which means long sales cycles, foreign sales teams and global competitors. Zoho and Freshworks, both from Chennai, made that leap; many others never could.

The second is gatekeepers. A toll-booth business pays tolls of its own: app stores take a cut of consumer revenue, telcos set the terms for business messaging, and Google and Meta can change ad rules overnight. These two together, a stingy home market and rent-seeking gatekeepers, explain most of the margin gap with American SaaS.

The third is AI, which is both rival and tool. It cuts the cost of writing code, which helps product builders. But it threatens any company whose moat was simply cheap engineers, and it threatens per-seat pricing.

Then the two stock killers. Services dressed as products: many listed names earn most of their revenue from implementation and customisation, billed by the hour, and the market pays a product multiple until the day it notices. And regulatory switch-offs: in 2025 the ban on real-money online games wiped out a whole category overnight, forcing gaming investors, Nazara among them through its stake in a poker platform, into write-downs.

In this sector one rule can delete a business model between Friday and Monday.

Rounding out the list: a talent war with foreign captive centres that pay more for the same engineers, a listing wave whose lock-in expiries weigh on prices, and data-localisation rules whose fixed costs favour the big.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck with its reason and a severity label. The labels group the risks into three kinds.

  • Structural: few large Indian buyers, platform gatekeepers, and AI as rival and tool. Three permanent rows, more than most industries carry. The so-what line singles out the first and third rows of the table, the home market and the gatekeepers, as the reason Indian margins trail American SaaS. These belong in your valuation.
  • Two-sided and recurring: services dressed as products, regulatory switch-offs, and the talent war. The so-what line calls the fourth and fifth rows, services in disguise and regulatory switch-offs, the stock killers. They are what to check name by name: read the revenue split between licence, subscription and services, and know which regulator can switch off the core product.
  • Cyclical and slow: listing-wave supply and data localisation. The first is a temporary drag on prices after a heavy listing year; the second a fixed compliance cost that slowly favours scale.

The useful habit is to run each company you own down the table. An enterprise name exports, so the first row has already been solved; its risk is the fourth. A payments platform worries about the fifth. A consumer app lives with the gatekeeper row every day. Different doors, different rows.

c8.story:
Software looks like the least regulated business imaginable: no factories, no pollution, no licences to make a spreadsheet. In India, that impression is dangerous. For half the doors in this industry, the rulebook decides whether the business exists.

Take payments. The RBI licenses payment aggregators, and since 2018 it has required payment data to be stored in India. A licence is a moat, because getting one is slow and expensive. But the RBI and the government also decide what a payment can cost. When UPI and RuPay debit payments were made free for merchants from 2020, an entire fee line disappeared for the industry by notification. Every payments investor now lives with the knowledge that a fee cap is one circular away.

Take gaming. In 2025 the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act banned real-money online games outright. Esports and casual games survived, but the real-money businesses, and the ad budgets they spent, vanished.

Take messaging. TRAI's rules require every business sender and message template to be registered on blockchain-based ledgers run by the operators. Platforms like Tanla earn from building that compliance plumbing, yet every tightening of anti-spam rules also cuts message volumes.

For a platform, the regulator can be your best customer and your biggest risk in the same year.

Some rules are pure moats. The Controller of Certifying Authorities licenses digital-signature issuers, a club of few members that includes eMudhra. The geospatial guidelines of 2021 freed Indian firms to collect and sell map data while limiting foreign players, the ground MapmyIndia stands on. Drone certification and a ban on importing foreign drones steer defence orders to Indian makers like ideaForge.

And over everything sits the new data protection law, whose Board started work in late 2025, adding consent and breach duties to every consumer app and ad platform.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule: what it does, why you care, and its status. The why column is where this card earns its keep, because in this industry it often names the company affected.

Read by status:

  • New: the data protection Act and its Board, and the online gaming Act of 2025. Both landed recently and both are still being absorbed: the first as a compliance cost and a possible squeeze on ad-targeting data, the second as a business that no longer exists.
  • Live: RBI payment-aggregator and localisation rules, TRAI messaging rules, the geospatial guidelines, and drone rules with their incentive scheme. These shape revenue now. Two are moats (maps, drones), two are double-edged (payments, messaging).
  • Always: MeitY IT rules with CERT-In directions, and the certifying-authority licence. Permanent fixtures: a fixed cost for most, a franchise for the licence holders.
  • Coming: US visa fees and tariffs, relevant to the product-plus-services names that still put engineers onsite.

A practical way to use the table: for each company you hold, find its row. A payments platform's row is the RBI one, and its risk is a fee cap. A messaging platform's row is TRAI's. A mapping or drone name has a moat row. If you cannot find a row for a company, its regulatory risk is mostly foreign: bank regulators abroad and data rules in its customers' countries.

Dated regulatory news for this industry sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces ask who keeps the money. In software, the answer depends almost entirely on one question: how painful is it for the customer to leave?

For the enterprise door, the answer is very painful. A bank that has run its loans, deposits and payments on one core system for years has woven it into every branch, every regulatory report and every staff habit. Switching means a multi-year project, a huge bill and the career risk of a failed migration. So the buyer, however large and tough, has surprisingly little power at renewal. Entry is just as hard: a core-banking product that regulators and auditors trust takes a decade to build, and the global shortlist, Oracle's Flexcube, Temenos, Finastra, FIS, Infosys's Finacle and a few others, rarely grows.

For platforms and consumer apps, the answer is not painful at all. An advertiser can move its budget next month. A student can leave one coaching app for another, or for a YouTube teacher. A merchant can swap a card terminal. And a new app, ad network or coaching channel takes a year to launch, not a decade. So rivalry turns into a fight on price and marketing spend, the kind that funded rivals love and shareholders hate.

Lock-in is the whole moat. Everything else is a marketing budget.

Two forces press on everyone. Suppliers, meaning engineers and cloud providers, have pricing power, especially when venture money is flowing and captives are hiring. And substitutes are real for both doors: AI-written software and in-house builds threaten enterprise products, while bundled offerings from the cloud majors threaten platforms. That is the one spoke where the two doors score the same.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes: global enterprise products, and platforms with consumer combined. The picture here is unusually clean. The platform-and-consumer shape is bigger on every spoke but one. It reaches the outer ring on rivalry and sits well out on suppliers, buyers and entrants. The enterprise shape is small and tucked in, smallest of all on entrants and buyers.

Look at the spokes in order of the gap between them:

  • Entrants shows the biggest gap: a decade to build a certified banking product, a year to launch an app.
  • Buyer and rivalry come next: a locked-in bank against a footloose advertiser or student.
  • Supplier is close: engineers and clouds squeeze both.
  • Substitutes is a tie, the one spoke where the shapes meet. AI and in-house builds threaten everyone equally.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with its reason. Read the buyer row's reason in particular; it is the whole investment case for enterprise software in one sentence.

The so-what line maps the shapes to profit: enterprise keeps it, platforms keep some while volumes grow, consumer keeps little until marketing stops being the biggest cost. If a consumer name you follow shows marketing falling as a share of sales, mentally shrink its rivalry spoke; that is the shape starting to change.

c10.story:
Product companies love metrics. Investor decks fill with monthly active users, annual recurring revenue, logos added and adoption curves. Eight numbers are enough to tell a real product business from a good presentation.

Start with recurring revenue growth in constant currency. One big licence deal can flatter a quarter; recurring revenue, subscriptions and maintenance, tells you whether the installed base is actually growing. Then employee cost as a share of sales, the single best test of whether a company scales like a product or bills like a service. A product company's ratio falls as it grows. A services firm's stays put, however many times the word platform appears in the annual report.

For platforms, the gross margin after pass-through is the number that matters, because headline revenue includes money that flows straight out to telcos, ad networks and banks. EBITDA margin then shows whether operating leverage is arriving or marketing is eating it.

A product company's employee cost falls as a share of sales. If it does not, you own a services firm with a better brochure.

Then the honesty checks. Receivable days: a jump means banks are paying slowly or revenue is being recognised ahead of cash. Capitalised development as a share of research spend: how much engineer cost is being parked on the balance sheet rather than expensed. If that share creeps up while employee cost falls, the improvement may be accounting, not scale.

Finally the two that measure the moat. Net revenue retention asks whether last year's customers spend more this year; above a hundred per cent means the base grows by itself, below it means churn is winning. And return on capital employed tells you whether the cash pile and the acquisitions bought with it earn their keep. Falling ROCE after a big acquisition is often the first confession of an overpayment.
c10.read:
Eight rows: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median from listed companies' latest annual filings.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask of every company you follow.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures. Several rows give separate marks per door: enterprise and platforms have very different healthy gross margins, because platforms pass so much through. Always apply the mark for the right door.
  • Today's median is the typical listed company. Two rows, capitalised development share and net revenue retention, show a dash: they come from notes to accounts and investor decks rather than the filing lines we hold. Dig those out yourself for the names you own.

Read the medians with three cautions. The growth median is reported revenue growth, not recurring revenue in constant currency, so a big licence deal or a currency swing can move it. The gross margin median comes from filings that do not always separate pass-through costs cleanly, so a platform's figure may look worse than its true business. And the median mixes all four doors, from banking software to coaching to drones, so it describes the industry, not any one model.

The best use of the table is a three-way comparison for each company: its own number, the median, and the good mark for its door. Pay most attention to the employee cost row: of the eight, it is the one that most directly separates the product companies from the services companies in disguise.

c11.story:
The earliest warnings for Indian software products are written in other people's results.

The loudest is the US software earnings season. When American software companies report and guide, two things happen: their multiples move, and Indian product names follow within weeks, and their commentary on enterprise budgets tells you what the banks and brands are planning. That arrives a quarter before Indian names report. The US ten-year yield speaks on the same horizon, moving multiples first and funding for rivals next. And Indian brands set their festive digital ad budgets a quarter ahead, which is when ad-tech volumes are really decided.

Two quarters out sit the slower voices. Global banks' commentary on technology spending tells you which core-banking and lending deals will be signed, since licences are booked well after decisions. Venture funding into Indian startups tells you whether funded rivals will soon be raising wages and discounting. And exam enrolments and new coaching centres tell you about edtech revenue across the next two quarters.

Some signals land the same quarter: the month's card and UPI counts for payment platforms, and any new RBI or TRAI rule, which changes volumes the quarter it lands.

Put the big signals together and you get the rule. The industry is in an up-cycle when US software multiples are rising, enterprise deal wins are growing year on year, and employee cost is falling as a share of sales. Today the first two are ticking: multiples are in a relief rally off the AI-scare lows, and banking-software deal wins are steady. The third is not: wage pressure keeps employee cost flat. Two of three, by the rule's own wording, means recovery.

A valuation bottom, not an earnings bottom: the revenue never fell, only the price did.

That is the call: prefer enterprise names with growing deal wins and usage-priced platforms over per-seat licences and consumer apps still buying growth, and let stock selection do the work while listing-wave supply clears.
c11.read:
The lead-time chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks; the further right, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for its channel.

  • Same quarter: card and UPI transaction counts, and RBI and TRAI rule notifications. These tell you what is happening to platform revenue right now.
